entries.title: Said to an observer
entries.locator: First PDF page, pp. 5–8
entries.body_html:
‘Anything said is said to an observer.’

Von Foerster adds this to Humberto Maturana’s proposition, Anything said is said by an observer. The person speaking and the person addressed both belong in the account. What happens between them matters.

Heinz von Foerster, Cybernetics of Cybernetics (1979), pp. 5–8; first page of the linked PDF. He explicitly credits Maturana for the first proposition and presents the second as his own corollary.

The familiar wording

“Everything said is said to someone” is the formulation in the discussion that prompted this page. It’s a useful paraphrase; the quotation above retains the paper’s wording.

entries.title: The ethical imperative
entries.locator: Final PDF page 13
entries.body_html:
‘Act always so as to increase the number of choices.’

Ask what your action makes possible, and for whom. My increased freedom may come at somebody else’s expense. Counting the options on a menu won’t settle that.

On Constructing a Reality (1973), final page. His later Ethics and Second-Order Cybernetics, pp. 288–289, distinguishes ethical commitments I make from moral commands imposed on others.

A first-person formulation

‘I shall act always so as to increase the total number of choices.’

This version makes the commitment personal. The circulating “Always increase the number of options” compresses the wording.

Disorder/Order: Discovery or Invention?. 1984, PDF p. 6, final paragraph before the discussion.

entries.title: The aesthetical imperative
entries.locator: Final PDF page 13
entries.body_html:
‘If you desire to see, learn how to act.’

What we can perceive develops through what we do. Participate, vary the action, and notice what becomes available to observation.

On Constructing a Reality (1973), final page. This accompanies the ethical imperative in the same closing passage.

entries.title: Meaning and the hearer
entries.locator: Item 4
entries.body_html:
‘The hearer, not the speaker determines the meaning of an utterance.’

Intending to communicate something doesn’t establish that it has been understood. Ask what the other person made of it. Their response changes what you can say next.

The 1995 anthology, item 4. This doesn’t release the speaker from responsibility for what they say.

entries.title: Not seeing the absence
entries.locator: Item 5
entries.body_html:
‘One does not see what one does not see.’

A blind spot doesn’t announce itself as a hole. Another person, a changed position, or an unexpected result may expose something your account had no place for.

The 1995 anthology, item 5, on the blind spot.

entries.title: Deciding the undecidable
entries.locator: Understanding Understanding, p. 293
entries.body_html:
‘Only those questions that are in principle undecidable, we can decide.’

Where an agreed framework compels the answer, it has already settled the question. Where it cannot, we have to choose and take responsibility. Evidence still matters; it cannot relieve us of every judgement.

Ethics and Second-Order Cybernetics, in Understanding Understanding (2003), p. 293. First published in French in 1991; the English journal version appeared in 1992.

entries.title: The missing observer
entries.locator: Printed p. 3
entries.body_html:
‘Objectivity is a subject’s delusion that observing can be done without him.’

The observer’s position, distinctions, and means of observing belong in the account. Acknowledging them creates obligations to explain and test a claim.

Bernhard Poerksen, The Certainty of Uncertainty, p. 3. Poerksen puts this attributed saying to von Foerster, who develops the argument in their conversation. This is the checked dialogue source, not a claim to have located its first use.

The 1984 essay also connects removing the observer from an account with avoiding responsibility. Read that argument, PDF p. 6.

entries.title: Ignored problems, fame, and success
entries.body_html:
‘The more profound the problem that is ignored, the greater are the chances for fame and success.’

A pointed question for any account of success: what had to be left outside it?

Responsibilities of Competence (1972), BCL #223, p. 1.

The Stafford Beer connection

Von Foerster says he presented the theorem at an earlier symposium and that Beer subsequently gave it its numbered name. The paper doesn’t establish a private exchange using the variant about ignoring more subjects and feigning success. That variant changes the wording and should be treated as a paraphrase.

The reported variant

“The more subjects you ignore, the greater your chance of feigning success” appears in Benjamin’s initiating post, attributed there to Heinz speaking to Beer. No primary passage for that wording has been located. It remains a reported variant.

entries.title: Hard sciences, hard problems
entries.body_html:
The “hard” sciences succeed with comparatively tractable problems; the “soft” sciences face harder ones.

His second theorem challenges an easy ranking of disciplines. Simplifying a social problem may remove the interactions that matter.

Responsibilities of Competence. 1972, p. 1, Theorem Number Two. Paraphrase of his contrast; the exact formulation is in the paper.

entries.title: Truth and the liar
entries.locator: Book title and publisher record
entries.body_html:
‘Truth is the invention of a liar.’

Follow this into the conversation about knowledge, certainty, and ethics. Using it as permission to disregard evidence would give the phrase rather too easy a life.

The title of Heinz von Foerster and Bernhard Poerksen’s book, subtitled Conversations on Epistemology and Ethics. The link is to the publisher’s record.

entries.title: The biologist belongs in the theory
entries.locator: The Single-Brain Problem, Theorem Number Three; reprinted on p. 195.
entries.body_html:
A biological account must also account for the living person who produces it.

This completes the paper’s three explicitly numbered theorems. A theory made by an organism must be able to accommodate that activity.

Responsibilities of Competence. The Single-Brain Problem, Theorem Number Three; reprinted on p. 195.

entries.title: Reality and community
entries.locator: Final PDF page 13, just before the two imperatives.
entries.body_html:
‘Reality = Community’

The closing equation makes room for other people in the account of reality. It precedes the ethical and aesthetical imperatives.

On Constructing a Reality. Final PDF page 13, just before the two imperatives.

entries.title: The perceived world as invention
entries.locator: Opening sentence, PDF p. 1.
entries.body_html:
The world we perceive is something we participate in producing.

This paraphrases the essay’s opening claim. The linked page preserves his precise formulation.

On Constructing a Reality. Opening sentence, PDF p. 1.

entries.title: The language of order
entries.locator: PDF p. 5, concluding sequence of propositions.
entries.body_html:
‘The length of descriptions is language-dependent.’

He links order and complexity to the descriptions an observer can produce. A changed descriptive language can change the apparent order.

Disorder/Order: Discovery or Invention?. PDF p. 5, concluding sequence of propositions.

entries.title: Necessity and chance
entries.locator: PDF p. 6, first paragraph; also anthology items 24–25.
entries.body_html:
Deductive certainty and inductive uncertainty concern our inference-making capacities.

His contrast places the observer’s abilities within the explanation of what appears necessary or accidental.

Disorder/Order: Discovery or Invention?. PDF p. 6, first paragraph; also anthology items 24–25.

entries.title: Closed organisation, open exchanges
entries.locator: PDF p. 6, discussion of autopoiesis.
entries.body_html:
An organisation can maintain its own organisation while exchanging energy with its surroundings.

Von Foerster explicitly credits Maturana, Varela, and Uribe in this discussion. Closure in one respect needn’t mean isolation in every respect.

Disorder/Order: Discovery or Invention?. PDF p. 6, discussion of autopoiesis.

entries.title: Learning to ask questions
entries.locator: PDF p. 6, Future, propositions 1–2 and preceding paragraph. Address 1971; publication 1972.
entries.body_html:
‘Education is learning to ask legitimate questions.’

Here the answer is not prescribed in advance. He credits Herbert Brün for this distinction and presents education as a necessity, beyond entitlement or privilege.

Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception. PDF p. 6, Future, propositions 1–2 and preceding paragraph. Address 1971; publication 1972.

entries.title: Better off together
entries.locator: PDF p. 6, Future, proposition 3.
entries.body_html:
‘A is better off when B is better off.’

The third proposition follows his account of education. Whose improvement is being pursued, and what happens to the other person?

Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception. PDF p. 6, Future, proposition 3.

entries.title: Vision and light
entries.locator: PDF p. 7, final sentence before the references.
entries.body_html:
‘Let there be vision: and there was light.’

He closes by reversing the familiar order: what becomes visible depends on the capacity to see.

Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception. PDF p. 7, final sentence before the references.

entries.title: Education and predictable answers
entries.locator: PDF p. 6, educational trivialisation before Future.
entries.body_html:
Testing only for prescribed answers measures how predictable a student has become.

The paper questions making predictability an ideal for people simply because it is useful in manufactured devices.

Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception. PDF p. 6, educational trivialisation before Future.

entries.title: Acting towards a future
entries.locator: PDF pp. 1 and 4.
entries.body_html:
An imagined future can orient present action; failing to act leaves others to act upon us.

Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception. PDF pp. 1 and 4.

entries.title: Observing myself
entries.locator: §8.45, printed p. 19; PDF p. 21.
entries.body_html:
‘I am the observed relation between myself and observing myself.’

A formulation of self-reference: the description includes the act of describing oneself.

Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things. §8.45, printed p. 19; PDF p. 21.

entries.title: The environment and information
entries.locator: §11, printed p. 23; PDF p. 25. Read alongside §10, PDF p. 24.
entries.body_html:
‘The environment contains no information. The environment is as it is.’

In §10, information depends on what an observer can infer from a description. The two propositions belong together.

Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things. §11, printed p. 23; PDF p. 25. Read alongside §10, PDF p. 24.

entries.title: Accounting for messages
entries.locator: §8 and §8.4, printed p. 18; PDF p. 20.
entries.body_html:
A communication theory must explain how messages arise, including the observer who identifies an interaction as communication.

Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things. §8 and §8.4, printed p. 18; PDF p. 20.

entries.title: Movement and logic
entries.locator: §9, printed p. 19; PDF p. 21.
entries.body_html:
Logical descriptions arise through organisms’ movements.

Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things. §9, printed p. 19; PDF p. 21.

entries.title: Constancy and change
entries.locator: §1.1, printed p. 11; PDF p. 13.
entries.body_html:
Constancy and alteration require each other.

Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things. §1.1, printed p. 11; PDF p. 13.

entries.title: The whole and its parts
entries.locator: Printed p. 266; PDF p. 6, after expression (12). Excerpt from a longer sentence.
entries.body_html:
‘the whole is neither more nor is it less than the sum of its parts: it is different.’

He is discussing the relationship between a recursive expression and the finite forms it entails. The difference matters more here than an arithmetic claim of superiority.

Objects: Tokens for (Eigen-)Behaviors. Printed p. 266; PDF p. 6, after expression (12). Excerpt from a longer sentence.

entries.title: Objects and stable behaviour
entries.locator: Printed p. 261; PDF p. 1. Presented in 1976; reprinted in 2003.
entries.body_html:
‘tokens for stable behaviors’

This is his phrase for objects in an account that includes the observer. Repeated sensorimotor coordination gives a route into the apparent stability of things.

Objects: Tokens for (Eigen-)Behaviors. Printed p. 261; PDF p. 1. Presented in 1976; reprinted in 2003.

entries.title: Tell me your universe
entries.locator: Metaphysics section, after the range of cultural accounts of origins.
entries.body_html:
‘Tell me how the Universe came about, and I tell you who you are!’

Accounts of the world also disclose their speaker. The question invites attention to the person making the account.

Metaphysics of an Experimental Epistemologist. Metaphysics section, after the range of cultural accounts of origins.

entries.title: Implicit ethics, explicit responsibility
entries.locator: Closing section, paragraph about the collapse of hierarchy.
entries.body_html:
‘ethics becomes implicit, responsibility explicit.’

His choice of language is part of how ethics is practised. The observer’s participation can’t be handed off to an external authority.

Metaphysics of an Experimental Epistemologist. Closing section, paragraph about the collapse of hierarchy.

entries.title: Expertise without disciplines
entries.locator: Opening answer. Stefano Franchi, Güven Güzeldere, and Eric Minch; Stanford Humanities Review 4(2), 1995. Public transcript mirror.
entries.body_html:
‘I don't know where my expertise is; my expertise is no disciplines.’

Academic labels can restrict what someone is allowed to investigate.

‘Disciplines are an aftereffect of the institutional situation.’

Interview with Heinz von Foerster. Opening answer. Stefano Franchi, Güven Güzeldere, and Eric Minch; Stanford Humanities Review 4(2), 1995. Public transcript mirror.

entries.title: Self-organisation needs an environment
entries.locator: Opening, printed p. 1; PDF p. 14. Essay published 1960, reprinted 2003.
entries.body_html:
‘There are no such things as self-organizing systems!’

The provocation challenges a system treated independently of the environment that supports it. Read the qualification with the sentence.

On Self-Organizing Systems and Their Environments. Opening, printed p. 1; PDF p. 14. Essay published 1960, reprinted 2003.

entries.title: Language as an invitation to dance
entries.locator: Answer to the question about reinventing language. Signed Santa Cruz, November 1999; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.
entries.body_html:
‘Language for me is an invitation to dance.’

Language is a joint activity in which both partners help shape the next step.

Christina Waters, Invitation to Dance: A Conversation with Heinz von Foerster. Answer to the question about reinventing language. Signed Santa Cruz, November 1999; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.

entries.title: It is how you tell it
entries.locator: Opening discussion of discovery and invention, after the journalism-school banner. Signed Santa Cruz, November 1999; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.
entries.body_html:
‘Nobody knows how it is. It is how you tell it.’

He uses this to insist on a writer’s responsibility for a description.

Christina Waters, Invitation to Dance: A Conversation with Heinz von Foerster. Opening discussion of discovery and invention, after the journalism-school banner. Signed Santa Cruz, November 1999; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.

entries.title: Inviting someone to see
entries.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The breaks of our conversation'. Conversation August 1998; published in the 2001 festschrift.
entries.body_html:
‘What matters to me is the invitation to see.’

Pörksen quotes this August 1998 conversation and says he recorded it. These are the words of the published English account; the recording itself has not been checked.

‘What the other sees is his business.’

Bernhard Pörksen, Beyond Distinctions: Memories of a conversation on Rattlesnake Hill about George Spencer-Brown and mystics. Paragraph beginning 'The breaks of our conversation'. Conversation August 1998; published in the 2001 festschrift.

entries.title: Learning how to learn
entries.locator: Section 'Non-causality', paragraph beginning 'Just prior to course registration'. 2001 festschrift; recollections begin in May 1959.
entries.body_html:
‘Learn how to Learn’

Inselberg asked what courses to take; this is the response he remembers.

Alfred Inselberg, HvF Recursion … or was it Magic?. Section 'Non-causality', paragraph beginning 'Just prior to course registration'. 2001 festschrift; recollections begin in May 1959.

entries.title: Helpful accidents
entries.locator: Opening section 'Skillful Good Fortune', paragraph beginning 'My timely arrival'. 2001 festschrift; recollections begin in May 1959.
entries.body_html:
‘skillful good fortune’

Inselberg says HvF regularly used the expression for helpful, otherwise mysterious coincidences. A characteristic phrase rather than a formal maxim.

Alfred Inselberg, HvF Recursion … or was it Magic?. Opening section 'Skillful Good Fortune', paragraph beginning 'My timely arrival'. 2001 festschrift; recollections begin in May 1959.

entries.title: Cherishing what is implicit
entries.locator: Paragraph beginning 'I remember many moments'. 2001 festschrift; individual contribution undated.
entries.body_html:
‘you must learn to cherish what's implicit in things’

Rebitzer recalls this advice in response to his persistent probing questions. The lowercase opening follows his text.

Robert S. Rebitzer, Doing Science. Paragraph beginning 'I remember many moments'. 2001 festschrift; individual contribution undated.

entries.title: The sons creating the fathers
entries.locator: Paragraph immediately after Scott describes his 1979 appreciation. Signed August 2001; telegram followed Scott's 1979 appreciation.
entries.body_html:
‘Congratulations! You have reversed evolution. Now the sons are creating the fathers!’

Response to Scott's tribute about cybernetics' founders. A joke about how later accounts create a field's ancestors, not a biological proposition.

Bernard Scott, Co-Creators: To Heinz from Bernard. Paragraph immediately after Scott describes his 1979 appreciation. Signed August 2001; telegram followed Scott's 1979 appreciation.

entries.title: Complexity and recursion
entries.locator: Paragraph contrasting recursivity and complexity, beginning 'Heinz looked on Luhmann's oeuvre'. 2001 festschrift; account of visits during 1990–1991.
entries.body_html:
‘If somebody is ignorant enough to want to deal with complexity, he will stay that way’

Baecker places the remark in a discussion of recursive operations and Heinz’s response to Luhmann’s work.

Dirk Baecker, The Eye of the Coyote. Paragraph contrasting recursivity and complexity, beginning 'Heinz looked on Luhmann's oeuvre'. 2001 festschrift; account of visits during 1990–1991.

entries.title: The value of another observer
entries.locator: Section III, paragraph beginning 'Earlier before the seminar'. 2001 festschrift; reconstructed exchanges from June 1971.
entries.body_html:
‘You are very valuable, because you see, you can be an observer.’

Welcoming a late arrival to the 1971 CIDOC seminar. Author explicitly warns at the beginning that he reconstructed conversations 29 years later.

Rodney Clough, “Getting” Heinz. Section III, paragraph beginning 'Earlier before the seminar'. 2001 festschrift; reconstructed exchanges from June 1971.

entries.title: An idea as a sculpture
entries.locator: Opening paragraph, within parentheses. 2001 festschrift; encounter in the mid 1980s.
entries.body_html:
‘an idea should be a sculpture!’

Galuszka remembers the phrase from their first meeting in the mid 1980s. His account leaves it unexplained.

Frank Galuszka, Perplexity. Opening paragraph, within parentheses. 2001 festschrift; encounter in the mid 1980s.

entries.title: Turning towards the green light
entries.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Heinz was arguing'. 2001 festschrift; author uncertain whether separate nighttime episode was in 1971 or 1974.
entries.body_html:
‘then I simply turn and go in the direction that is green.’

Schroeder remembers a classroom illustration: when a traffic light blocks a route, Heinz turns towards an open crossing. These words are the final clause of the recalled remark, offered as a way around an institutional confrontation.

Paul Schroeder, A Grasshopper Reflects. Paragraph beginning 'Heinz was arguing'. 2001 festschrift; author uncertain whether separate nighttime episode was in 1971 or 1974.

entries.title: How, why, and what
entries.locator: Scribe column, paragraph beginning 'He carried this into Pask's models'. Class-project material copyright 1972; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.
entries.body_html:
‘How, why and what refer to three different ways of relating things.’

Reproduced class-project material carrying a 1972 copyright. It is a scribe's account rather than an audio transcript.

Steve Sloan / reproduced student scribe and metascribe notes, Metagames. Scribe column, paragraph beginning 'He carried this into Pask's models'. Class-project material copyright 1972; reproduced in the 2001 festschrift.

entries.title: Talking to myself through you
entries.locator: Answer following the question about Maturana's languaging. Website post 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified and necessarily before HvF's death in 2002.
entries.body_html:
‘In a dialogue I am talking to me through you.’

Understanding changes as one's language returns through another person's response. English wording as published; interview date is not supplied.

Umberta Telfener, An interview to Heinz von Foerster (U.T.). Answer following the question about Maturana's languaging. Website post 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified and necessarily before HvF's death in 2002.

entries.title: Information as a change in relationship
entries.locator: Last paragraph before the concluding Taoist story. Website post 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified and necessarily before HvF's death in 2002.
entries.body_html:
‘Information is the way one changes after a relationship with someone.’

The interview treats information as a change in the person participating in a relationship.

Umberta Telfener, An interview to Heinz von Foerster (U.T.). Last paragraph before the concluding Taoist story. Website post 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified and necessarily before HvF's death in 2002.

entries.title: Questions that invite invention
entries.locator: Answers about therapeutic questions. Posted 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified.
entries.body_html:
Unexpected questions can require the answerer to invent a response and thereby become a poet.

Umberta Telfener, An interview to Heinz von Foerster (U.T.). Answers about therapeutic questions. Posted 20 February 2013; interview date unspecified.

entries.title: Knowledge and the reader
entries.locator: Answer on scientific and individual knowledge, before the concluding story.
entries.body_html:
Knowledge depends on the person interpreting a book, rather than passing intact from its pages.

Umberta Telfener, An interview to Heinz von Foerster (U.T.). Answer on scientific and individual knowledge, before the concluding story.

entries.title: Reading beyond current understanding
entries.locator: Final anecdote in Doing Science; the source itself uses indirect speech.
entries.body_html:
Rebitzer reports that Heinz recommended occasionally reading work beyond one’s current understanding.

There is no exact maxim to reproduce in this account. This is reported advice, retained as indirect speech.

Robert S. Rebitzer, Doing Science. Final anecdote in Doing Science; the source itself uses indirect speech.

entries.title: Questions, answers, and responsibility
entries.locator: Early answers on inventing and avoiding responsibility, before the language-as-dance passage.
entries.body_html:
He challenges the dismissal of questions as foolish, and criticises hierarchy and claims of having no choice as ways to evade responsibility.

Christina Waters, Invitation to Dance: A Conversation with Heinz von Foerster. Early answers on inventing and avoiding responsibility, before the language-as-dance passage.

entries.title: Now and here — a reader’s attribution
entries.locator: Opening paragraphs; November 2001.
entries.body_html:
‘everything is now and here’

Winter attributes this phrase to a small book he doesn’t identify and says he never met Heinz. The report is locatable; the book passage remains an open lead.

Wolfgang Winter, Everything is now and here. Opening paragraphs; November 2001.

entries.title: Not knowing at an examination
entries.locator: Oral-examination anecdote, after the retirement story.
entries.body_html:
‘I DON'T KNOW’

Kreitman recalls Heinz’s teasing advice to a doctoral candidate: let the examiners have the pleasure of explaining something. This is a remembered joke in a particular situation.

Kevin Kreitman, Some Heinz Stories. Oral-examination anecdote, after the retirement story.

entries.title: Computing a stable reality
entries.locator: PDF p. 11, Postulate of Cognitive Homeostasis
entries.body_html:
The nervous system’s organisation produces stability in experienced reality.

On Constructing a Reality (1973), PDF p. 11, Postulate of Cognitive Homeostasis. See also anthology item 22.

entries.title: Communication as recursion
entries.locator: Proposal 00, printed p. 308; PDF p. 321
entries.body_html:
‘Communication is recursion.’

The lecture develops this proposal into an account of mutual participation and stable patterns. Follow its numbered sequence.

For Niklas Luhmann: How Recursive is Communication?, proposal 00, p. 308. Richard Howe’s translation of the 1993 lecture, reprinted 2003.

index: Personal ethical wording; corrected deduction; uncertain geometry

other_series.title: Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things — all 12 main propositions
other_series.intro_html: The 1972 paper has 80 notes, organised around these 12 main propositions. Item 12 returns to item 1. This index covers the main sequence; the full text includes its subsidiary notes.
index: Constancy and alteration belong to representations
Formal representations across entities and instants
Objects and events as represented relations
Living systems maintain their own organisation
other_series.source_html: Read the original sequence, printed pp. 11–23 (PDF pp. 13–25). Proposition 7 draws on Maturana and Varela.

other_series.title: For Niklas Luhmann — every visible numbered entry
other_series.intro_html: The 1993 lecture’s checked 2003 translation has these eleven distinct labels. The repeated 00 stays one entry.
other_series.source_html: Read the full chapter, pp. 305–323. No 04 was located; 0.5 is preserved. Entry 02 has inconsistent determinability wording. Intervening discussions cover closure and stable outcomes. Borrowed material retains its named authors.

other_series.title: Responsibilities of Competence — all three numbered theorems
other_series.intro_html: Read the sequence together: ignored problems and success, the difficulty of scientific problems, and the biologist within a theory of biology.
other_series.source_html: Responsibilities of Competence (1972), opening and The Single-Brain Problem.

other_series.title: Perception of the Future — all three closing propositions
other_series.intro_html: The closing education sequence links inquiry with how people fare together.
other_series.source_html: Perception of the Future and the Future of Perception, PDF p. 6, Future.

scope: Complete topic index of the 1995 anthology, all 12 main propositions of Notes on an Epistemology for Living Things, every visible numbered proposition in the checked Luhmann chapter, and independently checked primary-paper additions and variants. No claim to contain every utterance by von Foerster.
